Because evolved does not mean good or fixed, we are entirely free to _judge_ our evolved tendencies and to _act against_ them, and we do so all the time, often at our best. A tendency toward aggression, even a deeply evolved one, is something a person and a society can recognize, disapprove of, and work to restrain. A bias toward our own group is something we can notice in ourselves and deliberately correct. Defeating the naturalistic fallacy is not a grim duty; it is what makes moral progress possible at all. If "evolved" did imply "good," we would be its prisoners. Because it does not, we are its judges.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: Is Is Not Ought: The Two Fallacies
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

_"If scientists say a behavior is evolved or natural, they're saying it's okay, or that we should accept it."_

This misreads what a scientific claim even is, and the confusion runs in both directions, which is why it is worth untangling carefully. When a researcher reports that some tendency appears to be an evolved part of human nature, that is a claim about _is_ : about what exists and where it came from. It carries no hidden "and therefore it's fine," any more than a doctor who tells you that the tendency to form arterial plaque is a natural consequence of human physiology is telling you that heart disease is "okay." Describing is not endorsing. The confusion does real damage in two ways. It makes some people hear every evolutionary claim as a moral approval and recoil (we will meet their specific error in a moment). And it lets other people _use_ evolutionary claims as smuggled approvals, dressing a value judgment as a neutral finding. The defense against both is the same clean move: when you hear "this evolved," refuse to let it mean anything more than "this exists and has an evolutionary history." What we should do about it is a separate question, on the far side of the gap, waiting for a value premise that the science cannot provide.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: Is Is Not Ought: The Two Fallacies
blocks.src:
### 4.3 The moralistic fallacy: unwelcome is not false

Now the second reader, whose error is less famous and, for exactly that reason, easier to commit unnoticed, because fewer people are watching for it. (The naturalistic fallacy, by contrast, is the more _notorious_ of the two and historically the more _consequential_ , as Chapter 17 will show when we reach the machinery of eugenics; the two are equally serious errors, dangerous in different ways.) To leap from "this claim would be harmful, offensive, or convenient for bad people _if_ it were true" to "therefore it is false" is the **moralistic fallacy**. It is the mirror image of the naturalistic fallacy: where the first slides from _is_ to _ought_ , the second slides from _ought_ back to _is_ , using a moral judgment to settle a question of fact.

The moralistic fallacy feels virtuous, which is what makes it so hard to resist. It arrives dressed as moral seriousness: _I refuse to believe something so ugly; believing it would make me complicit._ But wishing does not bear on truth. A claim about human nature is true or false depending on the evidence, and on nothing else. Its moral consequences, however dreadful, are simply not data about whether it is the case. To think otherwise is to believe that reality must conform to our hopes, that the world is forbidden from containing inconvenient facts, and a moment's reflection shows how dangerous that is: it means you have made yourself unable to _see_ any truth that frightens you, which is precisely the truth you most need to see clearly in order to deal with it.

This is the harder fallacy to teach, partly because the people most prone to it are often decent people with good intentions, and partly because calling it out can sound like siding with the unwelcome claim. So be very clear: pointing out that a frightening claim has not been _disproven by its frightfulness_ is not the same as asserting that it is _true_. The claim may well be false, on the evidence. The moralistic-fallacy warning says only that you must judge it _on the evidence_ , not by how much you wish it away. We will see in Part 6 that some genuinely false and pernicious claims have been resisted, by good people, with bad arguments, and that this is a gift to the people pushing those claims, who get to pose as brave defenders of forbidden truth against censorship. The most powerful refutation of a false claim about human nature is always the _evidence_ that it is false, never the announcement that it would be terrible if true.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: Is Is Not Ought: The Two Fallacies
blocks.src:
#### Definition: The naturalistic and moralistic fallacies

The **naturalistic fallacy** is inferring that because something is natural or evolved, it is therefore good, right, or acceptable (sliding from _is_ to _ought_). The **moralistic fallacy** is inferring that because something would be morally unwelcome if true, it is therefore false (sliding from _ought_ to _is_).

In plain language: the first says "natural, so fine"; the second says "unwelcome, so untrue." Both are wrong, both hop the is-ought gap, and they hop it in opposite directions. The naturalistic fallacy corrupts your _values_ by letting nature dictate them. The moralistic fallacy corrupts your _perception of facts_ by letting your values dictate them. A person who has truly internalized both can do something rare and valuable: look steadily at a frightening, well-supported claim about human nature, neither flinching away from its truth nor surrendering to its supposed implications, and then decide, as a free moral agent, what to actually do.


### 4.4 Holding both at once

The reason we install both fallacies together, in the same chapter, under the single banner of Thread C, is that you cannot safely hold one without the other. They are a matched pair, and people who guard against only one tend to fall straight into its twin.

Consider what happens if you watch only for the naturalistic fallacy. You become very good at insisting that "evolved" never means "good," which is correct. But unguarded against the moralistic fallacy, you slide toward treating _every_ uncomfortable evolutionary claim as not merely morally inert but factually suspect, dismissing science you dislike. You have escaped "natural so fine" only to land in "unwelcome so false." Now consider watching only for the moralistic fallacy. You become admirably tough-minded about following evidence wherever it leads, refusing to let squeamishness censor facts, which is also correct. But unguarded against the naturalistic fallacy, you drift toward treating whatever the evidence reveals about our nature as somehow _authoritative_ for how we should live, as though discovering a tendency were discovering a duty. You have escaped "unwelcome so false" only to land in "natural so fine."

The two fallacies are the two cliffs on either side of a narrow path, and the only way to walk it is to keep both in view at once. This is why, at every charged finding in the chapters ahead, we will do the same two-step explicitly: first establish, as carefully as we can, what _is_ the case (the science, judged by Chapter 3's toolkit, free from any wish about how it turns out), and then, entirely separately, ask what, if anything, _ought_ to follow (a moral question, answered by our values, to which the science contributes facts but never conclusions). We will draw the line between those two steps on the page, in plain sight, every single time. It will start to feel repetitive. Good. The repetition is the training. By the time we reach the most dangerous material in Part 6, drawing that line should be as automatic as the snake-flinch, and far more useful.


### 4.X Exercises

Thread C is a skill, and like any skill it is built by reps. These prompts are the first set. Notice that the work is almost never about the _facts_ in the scenario; it is about catching the illegitimate _move_ from fact to value or value to fact.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: Is Is Not Ought: The Two Fallacies
blocks.src:
#### Spot the Fallacy

**Q1.** For each statement, identify which fallacy (if either) is at work, and explain the illegitimate move precisely: (a) "Monogamy isn't natural for humans, so there's nothing wrong with cheating." (b) "Claiming humans have evolved status-seeking instincts is just an excuse for greed, so it can't be true." (c) "Our ancestors ate meat, so vegetarianism is unhealthy and wrong."

Hint

For each, find the factual claim and the value claim, then check which direction the inference jumps across the is-ought gap. One of these has a hidden extra problem beyond the fallacy.

**Discussion:** (a) is the naturalistic fallacy in plain dress: it slides from a claim about what is "natural" straight to "nothing wrong with" cheating. Even granting the factual premise (itself contested, as Part 4 will show), the conclusion does not follow, because "unnatural" does not mean "permissible" any more than "natural" means "good." Cheating's wrongness, if it is wrong, rests on broken promises and harm to a partner, considerations the naturalness of the urge does not touch. (b) is the moralistic fallacy: it reasons from "this claim would excuse greed" to "therefore it can't be true." But whether humans have evolved status-seeking tendencies is a factual matter for evidence; the worry that the claim could be _misused_ is a real worry about _use_ , not a refutation of the claim. Notice it might also be a category error to call status-seeking an "excuse for greed" at all, since describing a tendency never excuses acting on it. (c) is the naturalistic fallacy with an extra flaw bolted on: it leaps from "ancestors ate meat" to both a factual health claim _and_ a moral claim ("wrong"), and the factual leap is itself bad reasoning (what ancestors did is weak evidence about modern nutrition, given mismatch and the diversity of ancestral diets). So (c) commits the fallacy _and_ smuggles in an unsupported empirical claim, a reminder that real arguments often fail in more than one way at once.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: Is Is Not Ought: The Two Fallacies
blocks.src:
#### Sort the Claim

**Q2.** Someone says: "There's no such thing as human nature; the mind is a blank slate written entirely by culture, and any claim about evolved psychology is just ideology." Using Thread A _and_ Thread C together, what's the honest assessment of this statement?

Hint

First treat it as a factual claim (Thread A): is "blank slate" well-supported, contested, or refuted by evidence? Then ask whether the statement might be doing something other than reporting facts (Thread C): could the _appeal_ of "blank slate" be moralistic?

**Discussion:** Two passes. As a factual claim (Thread A), the strong blank-slate position is not well-supported; the convergent evidence (cross-cultural universals, infant abilities present before learning, the genuine heritability of psychological traits we will meet in Chapter 18) weighs heavily against the idea that culture writes on nothing. So as science, "the mind is a blank slate" sits closer to the _refuted_ end than the _open_ end, though the far more defensible claim nearby, that the mind is _highly_ flexible and culturally shaped, is true and important (Thread B). Now the second pass (Thread C): notice _why_ the blank slate is so attractive to many thoughtful people. It seems to guarantee equality and the possibility of change: if we are written entirely by culture, then no inequality is "natural" and everything can be reformed. That is a moral motivation, and a noble one, but if it is doing the believing, it is the moralistic fallacy at work, accepting an empirical claim because its implications feel safe. The honest assessment: the blank slate is largely false as science, and the wish to believe it (however decent) cannot make it true, _and_ , crucially, its falsehood does not endorse any status quo, because evolved is not good (the naturalistic fallacy still blocks that exit). This is the exact double-firewall posture the book is built to install, and we will return to this very statement, deepened, in Chapter 14.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: Is Is Not Ought: The Two Fallacies
blocks.src:
#### Steelman Both Sides

**Q3.** A scientist discovers strong evidence for some uncomfortable claim about an evolved human tendency. One colleague argues the finding should be published plainly, because suppressing true findings is corrosive to science. Another argues it should be published only with heavy emphasis on its limits and its non-implications, because in the real world such findings get weaponized and the harm is foreseeable. Steelman both, and locate exactly where they actually disagree.

Hint

Both colleagues accept the finding is true and both want to avoid harm. So their disagreement is not about _is_ and may not even be about _ought_ in the abstract. Where is it?

**Discussion:** The strongest case for plain publication: science depends utterly on not letting hoped-for conclusions filter which truths may be spoken, and the moment researchers start suppressing or burying findings because of feared misuse, they have surrendered to the moralistic fallacy at an institutional scale and handed every bad actor the priceless gift of posing as a censored truth-teller. Truth, plainly told, is also the only durable foundation for _correcting_ misuse. The strongest case for careful framing: findings do not enter a vacuum; they enter a world with a documented history of weaponizing exactly this kind of claim (Part 6), the misuse is foreseeable, and a scientist who can foresee predictable harm has some responsibility to forestall it, not by hiding the _is_ but by stating the _ought_ -firewall loudly alongside it. Now locate the real disagreement, which is the point of the exercise. Both colleagues agree the finding is true (no dispute about _is_). Both want to prevent harm (no dispute about the _value_ of avoiding misuse). They disagree about an _empirical_ question hiding inside the ethics: which publication strategy actually produces less harm in the real world? Does plain statement plus loud firewall inoculate the public, or does heavy hedging just look like exactly the evasiveness that fuels conspiracy? That is a question about consequences, answerable in principle by evidence about how people actually respond, not by which side feels more virtuous. The exercise teaches a subtle lesson: even a dispute that looks like pure values often has a factual question buried in it, and finding that question is how reasonable people make progress instead of trading accusations. This is the spirit in which Part 6 handles the field's most dangerous material.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: Is Is Not Ought: The Two Fallacies
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

We built the second firewall, the moral one, and it completes the toolkit we need to handle everything ahead. At its center is the is-ought gap: no statement of fact can by itself justify a statement of value, because crossing from _is_ to _ought_ always requires a value premise that the facts cannot supply. From that single principle fall the two fallacies that poison thinking about human nature. The naturalistic fallacy slides from _is_ to _ought_ ("evolved, so good or acceptable") and corrupts our values by letting nature dictate them; defeating it is what makes us free to judge and act against our own evolved tendencies. The moralistic fallacy slides from _ought_ to _is_ ("unwelcome, so false") and corrupts our perception of facts by letting our values dictate them; defeating it is what lets us see frightening truths clearly enough to deal with them. The two are a matched pair, the cliffs on either side of a narrow path, and guarding against only one drops you into the other. So we hold both at once, and at every charged finding we will separate, explicitly and on the page, the question of what _is_ from the question of what _ought_ to be.

With Chapters 3 and 4 complete, the full apparatus is now in your hands. Chapter 3 protects you from believing what is not true; Chapter 4 protects you from confusing what is true with what is good, in both directions. Only now, properly equipped, do we open the door to the wonders. Part 2 begins with the robust, low-controversy core of the field, where the science is strongest and the delight is purest, starting with the fear that flinched you away from a stick in Chapter 1. As you enjoy that material, and you should enjoy it, keep both firewalls lit. The wonders are real. So is the discipline that lets us hold them honestly.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: Evolved Fears
blocks.src:
Here is a fact that should puzzle you. Every year, cars kill more than a million people worldwide. Snakes kill far fewer, and although snakebite remains a serious killer in parts of the tropics, in most of the wealthy world your lifetime odds of dying by snakebite round to zero. By any rational accounting, you should break into a cold sweat at the sight of a speeding car and feel nothing at all about a snake. Yet the reverse is overwhelmingly true. Show people a snake and a modern danger like a handgun, and the snake tends to snatch attention faster, lodge in memory harder, and frighten children who have never been taught to fear it. The gun, a far deadlier object, tends to leave the ancient alarm system cold.

This is the cookie and the stick from Chapter 1, now under the microscope. We finally have the tools to ask the question properly. Is our readiness to fear snakes and spiders a genuine adaptation, shaped by selection because ancestral snake-fearers left more descendants? Or is it a just-so story, a tidy tale we tell because it sounds right? And if it is real, what exactly is real about it, because, as we will see, the honest answer is more interesting and more carefully bounded than the headline. This is also our first chance to watch the discernment toolkit of Chapter 3 do real work on a real case, and to see why "is it an adaptation?" almost never has a simple yes-or-no answer.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: Evolved Fears
blocks.src:
### 5.1 The case for prepared fears

The core idea is called **preparedness**. The proposal is that evolution did not hand us a fixed list of things to fear, nor a blank slate ready to fear anything equally. Instead it left us _prepared_ to learn certain fears far more readily than others: biased, pre-tuned, quick to acquire a dread of the things that actually threatened our ancestors (snakes, spiders, heights, deep water, strangers' angry faces) and slow or unable to acquire a comparable dread of things that are genuinely dangerous now but were absent then (cars, guns, electrical outlets). The danger that mattered for millions of years gets a hair-trigger; the danger that arrived last week does not.

Run this through Chapter 3's toolkit and notice how much better it fares than the blue-sky story we dismantled earlier. _Does it make risky predictions?_ Yes, and pointed ones. If preparedness is real, then fear of snakes should be learnable from a single frightening experience or even from watching someone else's fear, while fear of, say, flowers should not, no matter how you try to train it. People should detect a snake in a crowded visual scene faster than they detect a flower or a mushroom. Infants and even other primates should show a head start in attending to snakes. Each of these could have come out the other way, and so each is a real test.

_Does it converge with other evidence?_ Strikingly well. The attentional advantage shows up across cultures. It appears early, in infants who have had no chance to learn that snakes are dangerous. It appears in other primates, our relatives, who face the same ancient threat. And the bias is specific: the robust laboratory finding is that snakes are detected faster than evolutionarily neutral objects like flowers or mushrooms, and we show no comparable head start for modern dangers like guns, which is exactly the fingerprint an adaptation should leave and a general "we fear whatever hurts us" account cannot explain. This is the difference between a claim that has earned provisional belief and one that has only earned a shrug.


#### Definition: Preparedness

Preparedness is the proposal that natural selection biased humans (and other animals) to acquire certain fears more readily than others, pre-tuning us to learn quickly the dangers that recurred over evolutionary time while remaining relatively indifferent to equally or more dangerous modern hazards.

In plain language: we are not born afraid of snakes, and we are not blank slates that fear everything equally; we are born _ready to learn_ snake-fear fast and gun-fear slowly. Notice how this threads between the two cartoons we rejected in Chapter 1. It is not genetic determinism (the fear still has to be triggered or learned; plenty of people handle snakes calmly). And it is not the blank slate (the readiness is unequal, tilted by our history). It is a _tendency_ , in the precise sense we have been building: starting material, biased by the past, completed by experience. Thread B, evolved but not fixed, runs right through the middle of it.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: Evolved Fears
blocks.src:
### 5.2 Grading honestly: what is robust and what is shakier

Now we do the thing that separates this book from a pop-science article. We do not stop at "preparedness: confirmed." We ask which _parts_ of the preparedness story are well-supported and which are shakier, because the honest verdict is split, and learning to make that split is exactly the skill Thread A is for.

The strongest, most robust part is the **attentional and detection advantage**. The finding that snakes (and to a lesser extent spiders) capture human attention faster than neutral or even other threatening stimuli, that we are quicker to spot them, slower to look away, and more vigilant once primed, has held up well across many studies and many labs. This piece you can lean on. There genuinely does seem to be something in the human visual and emotional system that prioritizes ancestral creeping threats, and it shows the cross-cultural, early-developmental, cross-species convergence that marks a real adaptation.

But there is a second, more specific claim that does _not_ hold up nearly as cleanly, and the field's honest practitioners say so. This is the claim about **resistance to extinction** : the proposal that fears learned to snakes and spiders, once acquired, are unusually hard to _un_ learn, clinging on long after fears learned to neutral objects would have faded. The early experiments seemed to show this, and it became part of the standard story. But when later researchers tried to replicate the resistance-to-extinction effect carefully, the results came out inconsistent, sometimes appearing, sometimes not, in a way that does not support treating it as an established fact. The honest summary of this strand of the literature is that the evidence is mixed.

So the honest grade is a split verdict: **robust attentional effect, contested preparedness-conditioning mechanism.** The fast detection is real. The special un-learnability is doubtful. And notice, this is not an embarrassing climbdown or a sign the science is broken. It is the science working exactly as it should, with one component surviving scrutiny and another failing it. A field that could only say "snake fear: adaptation, yes" would be less trustworthy, not more. The willingness to say "this part holds, that part doesn't" is the mark of a discipline you can believe.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: Evolved Fears
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

_"Evolution proved we're hardwired to fear snakes, so being afraid of snakes is just human nature you can't change."_

Three errors are bundled in that one sentence, and pulling them apart is good practice. First, "proved" overstates: what is well-supported is the _attentional bias_ , while the stronger conditioning claims are contested, as we just saw, so the science is more textured than "proved." Second, "hardwired" smuggles back in the determinism we keep rejecting; preparedness is a _readiness to learn_ , not a fixed fear installed at birth, which is why many people feel no fear of snakes at all and why exposure therapy reliably helps those who do. The fear can be acquired, and it can be reduced. Third, and most important for Thread C, even the well-supported part is a claim about _is_ , not _ought_ : discovering that we are prepared to fear snakes tells us nothing about whether we _should_ indulge that fear, and indeed we routinely and rightly override it (the snake handler, the field biologist, the calm parent reassuring a frightened child). An evolved readiness is the starting point for what we make of ourselves, never the last word on it.


### 5.3 Fear as a constructed experience

There is one more layer to this, and it connects evolved fear to a theme that runs through the whole study of the mind. When you flinch at the stick-that-might-be-a-snake, it is tempting to imagine the process as simple: snake out there, fear in here, the eye like a camera passively reporting a danger that the mind then reacts to. But that is not how it works, and seeing why deepens everything in this chapter.

Your fear is not a readout of the world as it plainly is. It is a _construction_ , assembled rapidly by your brain from incomplete information, shaped by expectation and by the very biases we have been discussing. The curved shape on the path is genuinely ambiguous; it could be a stick or a snake, and the visual signal alone does not settle it. Your prepared, snake-biased system resolves that ambiguity on the dangerous side, fast and, on the leading account, largely _ahead of_ full conscious recognition, generating the experience of threat and the bodily flinch, and only afterward does slower processing arrive to confirm or correct. What you experienced as "seeing a snake and being afraid" was actually your brain building a fearful interpretation and acting on it, sometimes rightly, sometimes wrongly. The fear came first not because the snake was real but because your perception was already tilted to find one.

This is the same lesson that runs through the study of perception more broadly: the mind does not passively receive the world but actively constructs it, and evolution has tuned that construction toward ancestral priorities. Your snake-detector is not neutral. It is built to over-find snakes, because over-finding them was cheaper than missing one. Why that asymmetry, why a system _designed_ to make false alarms, is one of the most elegant ideas in the whole field, and it is the subject of Chapter 8. For now, hold the deeper point: even your fastest, most automatic fears are not raw contact with reality but interpretations, evolved interpretations, of an ambiguous world. The stick was never a snake. Your brain made one, briefly, because for ten thousand generations that was the safer mistake.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: Evolved Fears
blocks.src:
### 5.X Exercises

We are now grading real claims, with real split verdicts, so these prompts ask you to hold "robust here, contested there" in mind at once. The companion will use them to practice the fine sorting that separates this field's honest core from its overreach.


#### Sort the Claim

**Q1.** "Humans have an evolved fear of the dark." Run the toolkit, and be specific about what would count as evidence. Then compare your verdict to the snake case: are they equally well-supported?

Hint

What is the proposed ancestral danger, and is fear directed at darkness itself or at what darkness conceals? What cross-cultural, developmental, and comparative evidence exists, and is it as strong as the snake-detection data?

**Discussion:** Start by sharpening the claim, as always. Fear "of the dark" is probably better stated as a heightened wariness in conditions of _reduced visual information_ , where ambush predators and human enemies had the advantage over a daylight-adapted, vision-dependent primate. That is a reasonable adaptive hypothesis: it names a real ancestral danger and predicts that the fear should track _vulnerability_ (worse when alone, in unfamiliar places, when young) rather than darkness as an abstract quality. Run the toolkit. _Developmental evidence:_ fear of the dark is common in young children and tends to emerge around the age when an ancestral child would have become mobile and vulnerable, which fits. _Cross-cultural:_ nighttime wariness appears very widely. _But_ the evidence here is not as crisp as the snake-detection data, where we have controlled attention experiments, infant studies, and primate comparisons converging tightly. Darkness-fear is harder to disentangle from learned associations and from the simple fact that you genuinely cannot see threats in the dark (so some wariness is just rational, not necessarily a special adaptation). So the honest verdict: a _plausible and reasonably supported_ adaptive hypothesis, but graded a notch below the snake-detection bias, which has stronger and more specific convergent evidence. The lesson is that "well-supported" is not a single bin but a gradient, and intellectual honesty means placing each claim at the right point on it, not lumping all evolutionary fears together as equally proven.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: Evolved Fears
blocks.src:
#### Steelman Both Sides

**Q2.** On the resistance-to-extinction question (are snake-fears specially hard to unlearn?), steelman both the researchers who argue the effect is real and important, and the critics who argue it doesn't reliably replicate. What's actually at stake in this disagreement?

Hint

Both sides agree the attentional bias is real. The dispute is narrower. What would each side point to, and why does it matter for therapy and for theory?

**Discussion:** The strongest case for the effect being real: the original demonstrations were carefully done, there is a coherent theoretical reason to expect it (a fear system that was easy to switch _off_ would defeat its own purpose, since the snake that didn't bite you today can still bite you tomorrow), and several reviews conclude the resistance phenomenon is established. The strongest case for the critics: careful replication attempts have produced inconsistent results, and a finding that appears in some labs and vanishes in others has not earned the status of established fact, however appealing its theoretical rationale; we have learned, painfully, across psychology that theoretically pleasing effects sometimes fail to replicate, and the right response is humility, not loyalty. What is at stake? Theoretically, the strong version of preparedness (that evolution shaped not just _attention to_ snakes but a special _learning module_ resistant to extinction) rises or falls partly here; the weaker, attention-only version survives either way. Practically, it bears on therapy: if snake phobias really were specially extinction-resistant, that would predict they should be unusually stubborn to treat, yet exposure therapy works well on them, which is itself a piece of evidence against the strongest version. The honest resolution is the split verdict from 5.2: bank the robust attentional finding, hold the resistance-to-extinction claim as genuinely unsettled, and notice that the science is _more_ trustworthy, not less, for making the distinction.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: Evolved Fears
blocks.src:
#### Spot the Fallacy

**Q3.** A nature-documentary host says: "Our fear of snakes is ancient and hardwired, a gift from our ancestors that kept them alive. We should honor these instincts rather than override them with modern arrogance." What's wrong here, beyond the slightly overstated "hardwired"?

Hint

The phrase "should honor... rather than override" is doing moral work. Which fallacy turns an evolved instinct into something we _ought_ to defer to?

**Discussion:** Past the overstatement of "hardwired" (we have seen the science is a graded attentional bias, not a fixed installed fear), the host commits a clean naturalistic fallacy in the final sentence. "These instincts kept our ancestors alive, therefore we should honor rather than override them" slides from _is_ (we have an evolved fear-readiness) to _ought_ (we should defer to it), and the slide is illegitimate: an instinct's ancient usefulness in the EEA tells us nothing about whether deferring to it serves us _now_. In fact the chapter's own content refutes the host directly. Our prepared fears are calibrated to ancestral dangers, which is exactly why they misfire today, firing hard at near-harmless snakes while staying silent at lethal cars; "honoring" that miscalibration would mean fearing the wrong things. Overriding an evolved fear is not "modern arrogance"; it is often simple good sense, and the field biologist who calmly handles a venomous snake to study it is not betraying her nature but _using_ the rest of her nature (reason, learning, courage) to govern one part of it. The host has dressed a value judgment in evolutionary clothing, which is precisely the move Thread C exists to catch. Note the irony: the very flexibility that lets us override the fear is itself part of our evolved equipment, so even "honor your instincts" cannot tell you _which_ instinct to honor.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: Evolved Fears
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

We took the snake-flinch from Chapter 1 and put it through the full apparatus. The proposal of preparedness, that evolution left us biased to learn ancestral fears (snakes, spiders, heights) far faster than modern ones (cars, guns), fared well under Chapter 3's toolkit: it makes risky predictions and converges with cross-cultural, infant, and cross-species evidence, the fingerprints of a real adaptation rather than a just-so story. But we refused the lazy headline and graded honestly, arriving at a split verdict: the _attentional and detection advantage_ is robust and well-supported, while the stronger claim of _resistance to extinction_ (that snake-fears are specially hard to unlearn) replicates inconsistently and remains contested. That split is not a weakness of the science but a sign of its honesty. We kept Thread C lit throughout: even the robust findings describe what _is_ , never what we _ought_ to fear, and we override our evolved fears routinely and rightly. And we saw that even our fastest fear is not raw contact with the world but a _construction_ , an evolved interpretation of an ambiguous signal, tilted by ancient priorities toward the safer mistake of over-finding the threat.

That last idea, a perception system built to make systematic false alarms, is a thread we will pull hard in Chapter 8, where it becomes one of the most elegant principles in the field. But first, Chapter 6 turns to another ancient guardian of the body, one that protects against an enemy too small to see: disgust, and the immune system that runs not in your blood but in your behavior. As with fear, we will find a robust core, a speculative fringe, and a moral edge that demands the firewall. The wonders of Part 2 are real. We are learning to enjoy them with our eyes open.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: Disgust and the Behavioral Immune System
blocks.src:
A glass of apple juice sits in front of you. You take a sip; it is delicious. Now I dip a brand-new, sterile, freshly-unwrapped fly-swatter into the glass, the kind sold sealed in plastic, never used, with no fly ever near it. I stir once and remove it. The juice is, by any chemical measure, exactly as clean as before. Will you finish the glass?

Almost no one will. The thought alone may have produced a small recoil. And that recoil is fascinating, because it is so obviously _irrational_ in the narrow sense: nothing harmful entered the juice, you know nothing harmful entered the juice, and yet a wave of revulsion overrides the knowledge completely. The mere _association_ with something that contacts filth was enough. This is disgust, and like the snake-flinch it is a window into an ancient guardian of the body, one that protects you not from predators but from an enemy your ancestors could never see: the world of microbes, parasites, and rot that has been trying to eat us, and live in us, for as long as there have been animals.

In the last chapter we met an evolved defense against visible danger. This chapter takes up an evolved defense against _invisible_ danger, and it turns out to be one of the most robust and elegant findings in the whole field. But disgust also reaches, strangely, into morality and social life, into who we find repulsive and what customs we treat as defiling, and there the science gets more speculative and the moral stakes rise sharply. So once again we will sort the robust core from the speculative fringe, and keep the firewall lit where it matters.


### 6.1 The immune system you can see

Your body has a magnificent internal immune system: white cells, antibodies, fever, the whole biochemical war that fights pathogens once they get inside you. But fighting an invader after it has breached the walls is costly and dangerous. Far better, where possible, to never let it in. And that is a _behavioral_ problem, not a biochemical one. It requires detecting the cues of contamination out in the world (rotten smells, the look and feel of decay, bodily wastes, signs of illness in others) and then _doing_ something: recoiling, refusing, washing, avoiding. Evolutionary researchers call this first line of defense the **behavioral immune system** , and disgust is its central emotion.

Look at what disgusts people across the world and the pattern leaps out: it is a catalogue of ancestral infection risks. Feces, vomit, urine, blood and other bodily fluids. Rotting flesh and spoiled food. Creatures associated with filth and disease, like maggots, flies, and rats. Open wounds and signs of sickness in other people. These are not random aversions. They are precisely the things that, for our ancestors, carried a high load of pathogens, and the emotion that turns us away from them is doing exactly the job a behavioral immune system should: keeping the invaders out before the biochemical war ever has to start.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: Disgust and the Behavioral Immune System
blocks.src:
#### Definition: The behavioral immune system

The behavioral immune system is the suite of evolved psychological mechanisms (centered on the emotion of disgust) that detect cues of pathogens and parasites in the environment and motivate avoidance, reducing the chance of infection before the body's physiological immune system is engaged.

In plain language: it is the part of your mind that keeps you from eating the rotten thing, touching the sick person, or finishing the fly-swatter juice, a disease-avoidance system that works through behavior and feeling rather than antibodies. Run it through Chapter 3's toolkit and it passes impressively. It shows _special design_ : disgust is finely tuned to genuine contamination cues and follows sensible rules (contamination spreads by contact, a tiny amount of contaminant ruins a large amount of food, the effect is hard to reverse) that mirror how pathogens actually behave. It is _cross-culturally universal_ , present in every human society, with the same core triggers everywhere even as the details vary. It _appears in development_ on a sensible schedule. And it makes _risky predictions_ that have held up, such as that disgust sensitivity should rise when people feel more vulnerable to infection. This is the robust core, and it is robust indeed.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: Disgust and the Behavioral Immune System
blocks.src:
### 6.2 The reach into the moral and the social

Now the strange part, and the part where we must slow down. Disgust does not stay neatly in the domain of rotten meat. The same emotion, the same facial expression, the same recoil, shows up in places that have nothing obvious to do with pathogens. People speak of being disgusted by betrayal, by cruelty, by certain moral violations. They speak of "dirty" deeds and "purity," of being "sickened" by a politician's corruption. And, far more troublingly, disgust has historically attached itself to _groups of people_ : outsiders, the foreign, the stigmatized, those marked as somehow contaminating. What is going on when an emotion built to avoid spoiled food gets pointed at a moral act or a human being?

There are two broad possibilities, and the honest answer is that we do not fully know which is right, which is itself the lesson. One possibility is that moral and social disgust are genuine _extensions_ of the pathogen-avoidance system, evolution repurposing an existing emotion to police social and moral boundaries (treating cheaters and outsiders, who posed real social "contamination" risks, with the same recoil reserved for rot). On this view moral disgust is a kind of adaptation built atop an older one. The other possibility is that moral and social disgust are largely _byproducts_ and _metaphors_ : we borrow the vivid language and feeling of physical revulsion to express strong moral disapproval, the way we say a sneaky person is "slimy" without thinking they are literally covered in slime, and the brain reuses old emotional machinery for new, culturally-shaped purposes. Spandrel or adaptation, in Chapter 3's terms. The evidence is genuinely mixed, and careful researchers disagree.

What we can say with more confidence is that wherever it comes from, social disgust is _real in its effects_ and _dangerous in its uses_ , and this is where the firewall must blaze. Across history, the language and feeling of disgust, the casting of a group as filthy, verminous, contaminating, has been a reliable accompaniment to persecution. That is a fact about _is_ : disgust can be directed at people, and it has been, with horrific results. But notice the two errors waiting on either side. The naturalistic fallacy whispers that because disgust toward outsiders may have an evolved root, such revulsion is natural and therefore acceptable, which is monstrous and false: an evolved capacity to dehumanize is exactly the kind of evolved tendency we should recognize precisely so that we can _refuse_ it. And the moralistic fallacy whispers from the other side that because the idea of evolved group-disgust is so ugly, it must be scientifically false, which would blind us to a real and dangerous feature of our psychology that we urgently need to see clearly in order to guard against. Hold both. The capacity may be real _and_ the use of it may be evil, with no contradiction, because _is_ is not _ought_.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: Disgust and the Behavioral Immune System
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

_"Disgust is just a learned cultural reaction; different cultures find different things gross, so it can't be evolved."_

This sets up a false choice that we can now dismantle cleanly, because it confuses _variation in the details_ with _absence of a core_ , a confusion Thread B helps us avoid. It is perfectly true that cultures differ in what specifically disgusts them: a food relished in one society (fermented fish, insects, blood sausage, aged cheese that smells of feet) repels another. But look underneath the variable details and the universal structure is unmistakable: every culture has disgust, every culture centers it on the same core domains (bodily waste, decay, disease, certain animals), and the _rules_ of contagion are the same everywhere. What varies is the dial settings, calibrated by local experience about which specific things are safe or risky; what does not vary is the system itself. This is the signature of a _prepared_ mechanism, exactly like the prepared fears of Chapter 5: an evolved core that learning then tunes to local conditions. Neither pure instinct nor pure culture, but the interplay of the two, which is the real story of almost everything in this book. The cultural variation does not refute the evolutionary account; it is precisely what the evolutionary account predicts.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: Disgust and the Behavioral Immune System
blocks.src:
### 6.3 Disgust, vulnerability, and the modern world

One of the most striking confirmations of the behavioral-immune-system idea is also one of its more unsettling implications, and it shows the framework making a risky prediction that came true. If disgust is a disease-avoidance system, then it should get _stronger_ when the body is more vulnerable to infection and has less margin to fight one off. And it does. Disgust sensitivity tends to rise, for example, during the early stages of pregnancy, when the developing embryo is most vulnerable to toxins (and, on a separate and more tentative strand, when a woman's immune function is thought to be partly suppressed to tolerate the fetus), a pattern we will look at more closely in the next chapter. The system dials itself up exactly when the stakes are highest. That is the kind of specific, functional fine-tuning that marks a genuine adaptation and that a "disgust is just learned" account cannot explain.

But the same sensitivity that protected our ancestors can misfire in the modern world, in ways that matter morally and politically, and here we must be careful to describe without prescribing. Because the behavioral immune system works by crude, fast, better-safe-than-sorry cues (it would rather wrongly avoid a healthy stranger than risk contact with a sick one), it can generate avoidance of people who merely _look_ unfamiliar, who bear harmless differences the ancient system misreads as disease cues, or who belong to groups culturally coded as "contaminating." Some research suggests that feelings of disease-vulnerability can nudge attitudes toward greater wariness of outsiders and stronger preference for the familiar, though the robustness of this specific effect is itself debated. This is a claim about _is_ , and it is sobering. But its lesson is the opposite of resignation. If a fraction of human prejudice runs on a miscalibrated disease-avoidance reflex firing at the wrong targets, then understanding that reflex is a tool for _disarming_ it: recognizing the recoil for the ancient false alarm it often is, and refusing to let a system built for rotten meat decide how we treat human beings. Evolved, but not fixed. Described, but never endorsed. The science illuminates the trap; our values, not our reflexes, decide whether we fall into it.


### 6.X Exercises

These prompts work the seam between disgust's robust core and its contested social reach, which is exactly the kind of "robust here, speculative there, dangerous over here" terrain the whole book is training you to navigate.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: Disgust and the Behavioral Immune System
blocks.src:
#### Sort the Claim

**Q1.** "Moral disgust (feeling sickened by cruelty or betrayal) is an evolved adaptation that helped our ancestors police social rules." Where does this land: well-supported, contested, or story? How does it compare to the claim that _physical_ disgust at rotten food is an adaptation?

Hint

The physical-disgust claim passed the toolkit cleanly in 6.1. Does the moral-disgust claim have the same special-design, cross-cultural, developmental, and risky-prediction support? Or is the adaptation-versus-byproduct question still genuinely open?

**Discussion:** The two claims sit in very different places, and seeing why is the point. Physical disgust at contamination is _well-supported_ : special design, cross-cultural universality, developmental schedule, and confirmed risky predictions (the vulnerability effect) all converge. Moral disgust is _genuinely contested_. The honest difficulty, from 6.2, is that we cannot yet cleanly distinguish two live hypotheses: that moral disgust is a real evolutionary _extension_ of the pathogen system (an adaptation built on an adaptation), or that it is largely a _byproduct and metaphor_ , borrowing the feeling and language of physical revulsion for culturally-shaped moral purposes. Both are plausible; the evidence does not decisively favor one; careful researchers disagree. So the right verdict is not "yes, adaptation" or "no, just metaphor" but "the _phenomenon_ is real (people do feel moral disgust) and its _evolutionary status_ is open, with adaptation and byproduct both still on the table." Notice this is a more sophisticated use of Thread A than the snake case: there the split was between two empirical findings (attention robust, extinction contested); here the split is between an agreed phenomenon and a contested _explanation_ of it. Learning to say "the pattern is real but its evolutionary interpretation is unsettled" will be the single most common honest verdict in the charged chapters ahead, and this is good practice for it.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: Disgust and the Behavioral Immune System
blocks.src:
#### Spot the Fallacy

**Q2.** A pundit argues: "Humans evolved to feel disgust toward outsiders as a defense against foreign diseases. So hostility to immigrants isn't bigotry, it's a natural protective instinct, and trying to suppress it is fighting human nature." Dismantle this carefully, in both factual and moral terms.

Hint

There are at least two distinct problems: a possible overstatement of the _is_ (how solid is the factual premise?), and a clear illegitimate move to the _ought_. Address both, and don't let fixing one make you commit the opposite fallacy.

**Discussion:** Attack it on both fronts, carefully, because this is exactly the kind of argument the whole book is built to defuse. First the _is_. The factual premise is stated far too confidently: as 6.2 and 6.3 showed, whether group-directed disgust is a genuine adaptation or a misfiring byproduct of the pathogen system is _contested_ , not established, so "humans evolved to feel disgust toward outsiders" overstates a real but uncertain hypothesis as settled fact, smuggling false confidence in to do moral work. But, and this is the crucial discipline, we must not over-correct into the moralistic fallacy by declaring the factual claim _false because it is ugly_ ; the honest line is that it is _uncertain_ , and that uncertainty is part of the rebuttal. Now the _ought_ , where the pundit commits a flagrant naturalistic fallacy: even if the disease-avoidance-misfiring account were _fully confirmed_ , "this hostility has an evolved root" would tell us exactly nothing about whether we should _indulge_ it. The chapter's own logic cuts the other way. If hostility to immigrants runs partly on a crude reflex built for rotten meat and firing at the wrong target, then it is a _false alarm_ , a miscalibration, precisely the kind of evolved tendency our reason and values should override, not obey. The pundit has taken a contested _is_ , inflated it to a certain one, and then leapt across the gap to an _ought_ it could never support. Factually overconfident, morally fallacious, and refuted by the very science it invokes.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: Disgust and the Behavioral Immune System
blocks.src:
#### Steelman Both Sides

**Q3.** Steelman both positions in the scholarly debate from 6.2: (a) moral and social disgust are genuine evolutionary extensions of the pathogen-avoidance system; (b) they are byproducts and metaphors, the reuse of old emotional machinery for culturally-constructed purposes. What kind of evidence would help decide between them?

Hint

What does each side predict about how moral disgust should behave: should it follow the contagion rules of physical disgust, share its physiology, develop on the same schedule? Where the two predictions diverge is where evidence can bite.

**Discussion:** The strongest case for (a), genuine extension: moral and social disgust share a great deal with physical disgust, including the same characteristic facial expression, overlapping bodily and neural responses, and a tendency to follow contagion-like rules (moral "taint" spreading by association, purification rituals to remove it), which is what you would expect if evolution had recruited the old system to a new policing job that mattered for ancestral social life. There is also a coherent functional story: outsiders and rule-breakers really did pose contamination-like risks (disease, social exploitation), so a system that recoiled from them could have paid. The strongest case for (b), byproduct and metaphor: humans constantly borrow concrete sensory language for abstract domains (we speak of "warm" people and "heavy" news without literal temperature or weight), so "sickening" cruelty may be just another such metaphor riding on vivid old machinery; moreover, _what_ counts as morally disgusting varies enormously across cultures and history in ways that look more like cultural construction than like a tuned adaptation, and some studies find that moral and physical disgust dissociate under closer testing. What evidence would help? Tests of whether moral disgust truly obeys the _specific_ contagion rules of physical disgust or only loosely resembles them; developmental work on whether moral disgust emerges on an evolutionary-looking schedule or tracks cultural learning; careful physiological and neural studies probing whether the two are the same system or merely similar. The exercise's real lesson is that "is it an adaptation?" is often answerable only by finding where the rival hypotheses make _different_ predictions, which is the discipline that keeps Thread A from collapsing into mere opinion.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: Disgust and the Behavioral Immune System
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

We met an ancient guardian against an invisible enemy. Disgust is the central emotion of the _behavioral immune system_ , an evolved first line of defense that detects the cues of pathogens (waste, decay, disease, the creatures of filth) and turns us away before infection can begin. This robust core passes Chapter 3's toolkit cleanly: special design, cross-cultural universality, a sensible developmental course, and confirmed risky predictions like the rise of disgust sensitivity when the body is most vulnerable. The fly-swatter in the juice showed how completely this fast, ancient system can override what we rationally know. But disgust reaches, strangely, into morality and social life, and there the science turns genuinely contested: whether moral and group disgust are real evolutionary _extensions_ of the pathogen system or _byproducts and metaphors_ borrowing its machinery is an open question, with adaptation and spandrel both still live. And there the moral stakes rise, because disgust directed at human groups has been a faithful companion of persecution. So we lit the firewall in both directions: an evolved capacity to dehumanize, if it exists, is exactly what we must recognize in order to _refuse_ (against the naturalistic fallacy), and its ugliness does not make it scientifically false (against the moralistic fallacy). The reflex built for rotten meat must never be allowed to decide how we treat people.

Notice the pattern repeating from Chapter 5 and deepening: a robust empirical core, a contested interpretive fringe, and a moral edge that demands the firewall. This is what honest work in this field looks like, and you are getting fluent in it. Chapter 7 stays in the body's ancient wisdom but turns from defense to appetite: the cravings for sugar, fat, and salt that once kept our ancestors alive and now, in a world of endless cheap calories, quietly harm us. It is the cleanest case of mismatch in the whole book, the cookie from Chapter 1 finally explained, and it carries its own temptation to slide from _is_ to _ought_ about how we eat. We continue, eyes open, through the wonders.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 7: The Sweet Tooth and the Modern World
blocks.src:
We finally return to the cookie. In Chapter 1 it stood for the whole puzzle of the book: a craving that outruns your hunger, a want that wins even when you know better. Now we can explain it, and the explanation is the cleanest case of mismatch in the entire field, so clean that it serves as the model for every other mismatch claim you will ever evaluate. Where the fear of snakes had a split verdict and disgust had a contested social fringe, the sweet tooth is about as solid as evolutionary psychology gets. Understanding it well is therefore double duty: you learn why diets fight biology, and you acquire a gold-standard example of what a _well-supported_ mismatch claim looks like, so that you can spot the overstretched ones later.

But even here, in the safest territory, the firewall matters. Because the moment we explain _why_ we crave what harms us, the temptation arrives to draw conclusions about how we _should_ eat, whom to blame for what they weigh, and what is "natural" for the human body. The science can tell us a great deal about the _is_ of appetite. It cannot, by itself, tell us a single thing about the _ought_ of how to live with it, and confusing the two has done real harm to real people. So we will enjoy the clarity of this chapter and keep Thread C lit even in the sunshine.


### 7.1 Why sweetness tastes like joy

Imagine the world your sense of taste was built for. Not a supermarket. A landscape where food was uncertain, often scarce, and where the difference between a good year and a dead one could come down to calories banked before winter. In that world, what should an animal's tongue be tuned to love? Exactly the things that were rare, valuable, and hard to get: concentrated energy and scarce nutrients.

And that is precisely what we love. _Sweetness_ signaled ripe fruit and honey, the richest bursts of quick energy available, and almost never signaled poison (toxic plants tend to be bitter), so a powerful pull toward sweet was a pull toward safe, high-value calories. _Fat_ was the densest energy source of all, the prize cut of a hunted animal, worth enormous effort, and we are built to find it deeply satisfying. _Salt_ was a scarce necessity the body cannot make and must find, so a strong appetite for it guided animals to a vital and limited resource. In the ancestral world, these cravings were not vices. They were a finely-tuned nutritional guidance system, steering a hungry animal toward exactly what its body most needed and could least reliably get. The craving that feels like weakness was, in its original setting, wisdom.

Now change one thing and hold everything else fixed: make those once-rare substances _unlimited and cheap_. Pile sugar into everything, render fat abundant, salt the whole food supply. The guidance system does not know the world has changed. It goes on shouting _yes, get that, more of that, this is the good stuff_ at a tongue now swimming in the very things it was built to chase across a hungry landscape. The result is not a broken system. It is a _working_ system, working exactly as designed, in an environment that violates every assumption it was designed for. That is mismatch, and the modern epidemic of diet-related disease is, in large part, its signature.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 7: The Sweet Tooth and the Modern World
blocks.src:
#### Definition: Evolutionary mismatch

Evolutionary mismatch occurs when a trait that was adaptive in the environment where it evolved produces harmful or maladaptive outcomes in a modern environment that differs from the ancestral one in some crucial respect.

In plain language: it is what happens when an old solution meets a new world it was never built for, so that the very feature that once helped now hurts, not because the feature changed but because the world did. The sweet tooth is the textbook case, and it is worth pausing on _why_ it is so clean, because that is the lesson. The ancestral problem is well understood (calorie scarcity). The adaptive logic is straightforward (crave the rare, valuable energy). The modern change is undeniable and recent (industrial food abundance). And the prediction is confirmed in detail (we overconsume exactly the substances the theory names, with exactly the health consequences it predicts). When all four of those line up, a mismatch claim is on solid ground. File this pattern; we will use it as the measuring stick.


### 7.2 When mismatch is real and when it is hand-waving

Here is the danger that lurks behind a concept as satisfying as mismatch: it is _too_ satisfying. Once you have the idea, you can explain almost any modern ailment by gesturing at the ancestral world. Anxious? Mismatch, our ancestors faced acute threats, not chronic stress. Can't focus? Mismatch, we evolved for the savanna, not the spreadsheet. Lonely? Mismatch, we evolved for small bands, not cities. Some of these may be partly true. But notice that the _form_ of the argument is exactly the just-so story of Chapter 3, wearing a fashionable new coat. "Mismatch" can become a magic word that explains everything and therefore explains nothing, and the discipline of this chapter is to tell the difference.

The sweet tooth is solid, we saw, because four things line up: a well-understood ancestral problem, clear adaptive logic, an undeniable recent environmental change, and a confirmed detailed prediction. Now watch how a weaker mismatch claim fails to meet that standard. Take "we are anxious because we evolved for acute physical threats, not modern chronic stressors." The ancestral problem is plausible but vague. The adaptive logic is loose (what exactly is the adaptation, and what precisely changed?). And the prediction is soft: almost any pattern of modern anxiety could be fitted to the story after the fact, which is the reversibility tell from Chapter 3. This does not mean the anxiety claim is _false_ ; it means it is _weaker_ , sitting closer to "plausible story" than to "well-supported finding," and an honest writer grades it that way rather than dressing it in the sweet tooth's credibility.

So mismatch is a real and powerful idea _and_ a favorite hiding place for the unfalsifiable story, just as we warned about the EEA in Chapter 2. The two cautions are the same caution. Whenever you meet a mismatch claim, run the sweet tooth's four-part test on it: Is the ancestral problem well understood, or just gestured at? Is the adaptive logic specific, or loose? Is the environmental change clear and recent, or vague? Is the prediction detailed and confirmed, or could the story fit any outcome? The strength of the claim is exactly how well it answers those four. The sweet tooth aces all four. Most mismatch claims do not, and saying so is not anti-evolutionary; it is Thread A doing its job in the field's friendliest territory.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 7: The Sweet Tooth and the Modern World
blocks.src:
### 7.3 Pregnancy sickness: a candidate adaptation

Let us look at one more appetite phenomenon, partly because it is genuinely fascinating and partly because it is a perfect intermediate case, more solid than the anxiety story but more contested than the sweet tooth, and learning to place such in-between cases is the whole art. The phenomenon is the nausea and food aversion that many women experience in early pregnancy, commonly called morning sickness though it is not confined to mornings.

The standard view treats it as an unfortunate side effect of pregnancy hormones, a malfunction to be endured. But an evolutionary hypothesis proposes something more interesting: that pregnancy sickness may be an _adaptation_ to protect the developing fetus during its most vulnerable period. The reasoning runs like this. The first trimester, when sickness peaks, is exactly when the embryo's organs are forming and most sensitive to toxins. The aversions tend to target precisely the foods most likely, in an ancestral world, to carry toxins or dangerous microbes: strong-smelling foods, bitter vegetables, meat. And recall from Chapter 6 that disgust sensitivity rises in early pregnancy too, which fits the same protective logic from a different angle. On this view the misery of morning sickness is not a bug but a feature: a system that makes the mother temporarily picky and queasy, steering her away from risk at the one moment when risk is most costly.

Run the toolkit. The hypothesis makes _risky predictions_ (sickness should track the period of maximum fetal vulnerability; aversions should target higher-risk foods; some marker of better outcomes might correlate with sickness), and several of these find support, which is more than a just-so story can claim. But the verdict is not as clean as the sweet tooth, because alternative explanations remain live (some of the pattern may be a byproduct of hormonal changes doing other jobs), the evidence is suggestive rather than decisive, and the details are still debated. So the honest grade is _promising candidate adaptation_ , a notch below the sweet tooth's near-certainty and a notch above the anxiety story's loose speculation. It sits in the middle of the gradient, and the right intellectual response is neither to present it as established fact nor to dismiss it, but to hold it as a well-motivated hypothesis with real but incomplete support. Practicing that calibrated, in-between judgment is more valuable than memorizing any single verdict.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 7: The Sweet Tooth and the Modern World
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

_"If our cravings for sugar and fat are natural and evolved, then eating them is just following our nature, and 'unnatural' processed diets are the only real problem."_

This packs a naturalistic fallacy inside a half-truth, and untangling it protects both your reasoning and, frankly, real people from real harm. The half-truth: yes, the cravings are evolved, and yes, the modern food environment is genuinely novel in ways that matter (the mismatch is real). But watch the illegitimate moves. "Eating them is just following our nature" slides from _is_ (we crave these) to a quiet _ought_ (so indulging is fine, or at least not our responsibility), and that slide is exactly the naturalistic fallacy: that a craving is evolved tells us nothing about whether acting on it serves our health or our goals now. The same logic that explains the craving also explains why _overriding_ it is often wise, since the craving is calibrated to a vanished world. And the flip side, romanticizing "natural" diets, commits the fallacy in the other direction, treating "ancestral" as a synonym for "healthy" when ancestral diets varied enormously, were often precarious, and were optimized for survival-to-reproduction in scarcity, not for a long, comfortable modern lifespan. The deepest error, though, is moral, and worth naming plainly: understanding the evolved roots of appetite should increase our _compassion_ , not our judgment. A person fighting a sugar craving is fighting ten thousand generations of finely-tuned biology in an environment engineered to exploit it; that is a fact about _is_ that should inform how we treat ourselves and others, while leaving every question of _ought_ (how to eat, how to design food policy, how to regard our own bodies) exactly where it belongs, on the human side of the gap.


### 7.X Exercises

These prompts drill the chapter's central skill: distinguishing a rock-solid mismatch claim from a hand-waving one, and keeping the firewall lit even when the science is friendly.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 7: The Sweet Tooth and the Modern World
blocks.src:
#### Sort the Claim

**Q1.** Rank these three mismatch claims from best-supported to weakest, and justify the ranking with the four-part test from 7.2: (a) "We crave sugar because it was scarce and valuable ancestrally"; (b) "We get short-sighted (myopia) at modern rates partly because close-up indoor work and lack of daylight differ from ancestral visual environments"; (c) "We're unhappy at work because we evolved to be hunter-gatherers, not to sit at desks."

Hint

For each, ask: ancestral problem well understood? adaptive logic specific? environmental change clear and recent? prediction detailed and confirmed? Don't assume "weaker" means "false."

**Discussion:** Best-supported is (a), the sugar claim, which aces all four parts as 7.1 detailed; it is the gold standard. Weakest is (c), the desk-job-unhappiness claim, which fails or only loosely passes most of the test: the "adaptation" is vague (we did not evolve a specific "be a hunter-gatherer" module), the environmental change is real but the causal chain to "unhappiness at work" is loose and multiply-determined, and the prediction is so soft that almost any pattern of job satisfaction could be retrofitted to it (the reversibility tell). That does not make it false; people may well be happier with variety and autonomy than with monotonous confinement, but as stated it is a plausible _story_ , not a well-supported finding. The interesting case is (b), myopia, which sits in the middle and surprises people: there is genuinely suggestive evidence that reduced exposure to bright outdoor daylight in childhood is associated with the modern rise in short-sightedness, the environmental change is clear and recent, and the prediction is reasonably specific (outdoor-light exposure tracks myopia rates, though the exact mechanism is still being worked out). So the honest ranking is (a) strongest, (b) genuinely supported and more solid than it first sounds, even though its own verdict is still moving, (c) weakest and closer to story. The lesson: do not rank by how _evolutionary_ the claim sounds or how appealing it feels; rank by how well it survives the four-part test. The desk-job claim sounds the most sweepingly "evolutionary" and is the weakest of the three.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 7: The Sweet Tooth and the Modern World
blocks.src:
#### Spot the Fallacy

**Q2.** A wellness influencer says: "Your body evolved to crave fat and sugar, so restrictive diets fight your natural wisdom. Listen to your cravings, they evolved to keep you healthy." Find every error.

Hint

There's a naturalistic fallacy, but also a factual error about _what the cravings were calibrated for_ and _what environment they assume_. The cravings did evolve to keep ancestors healthy, in a specific setting. Is that setting yours?

**Discussion:** This one is almost a trap, because it contains a true premise that makes the false conclusion feel earned. True: your cravings did evolve, and in the ancestral environment they did promote health by steering you toward scarce, valuable calories. The errors begin immediately after. Factually, the influencer ignores mismatch entirely: the cravings were calibrated for a world of _scarcity_ , so "listen to your cravings" is good advice in that world and potentially harmful advice in a world of engineered abundance, where the same signals now overshoot. The phrase "natural wisdom" treats the craving as if it were tracking your _current_ health, when it is actually tracking an _ancestral_ problem that no longer exists in the same form, which is precisely why it misleads. Morally, "restrictive diets fight your natural wisdom" is a naturalistic fallacy: even granting the cravings are natural, nothing follows about whether indulging or restraining them serves you now; "natural" is not "healthy" and certainly not "obligatory." Notice the influencer has done something subtly clever and dishonest: used a _correct_ evolutionary fact (cravings evolved to promote health) while silently dropping the _crucial qualifier_ (in an environment unlike yours), then crossed the is-ought gap on top of the resulting half-truth. The most insidious naturalistic-fallacy arguments are exactly these, the ones built on a real finding with the context quietly removed. Spotting the missing qualifier is as important as spotting the fallacy.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 7: The Sweet Tooth and the Modern World
blocks.src:
#### Steelman Both Sides

**Q3.** Pregnancy sickness: steelman both the view that it is a protective adaptation and the view that it is mainly a byproduct of pregnancy hormones doing other jobs. What evidence would push you toward one?

Hint

The adaptation view predicts functional fine-tuning (timing, targets, outcomes). The byproduct view predicts the pattern should be explained by hormonal mechanisms without needing a protective function. Where do their predictions diverge?

**Discussion:** The strongest case for _adaptation_ : the timing is suspiciously functional (sickness peaks exactly when the embryo is most vulnerable to toxins and eases as that window closes), the aversions target the right foods (those historically likely to carry toxins or pathogens), the parallel rise in disgust sensitivity (Chapter 6) points the same way, and there is some evidence linking sickness to pregnancy outcomes, all of which is the kind of specific, converging, functional fine-tuning that marks design rather than accident. The strongest case for _byproduct_ : pregnancy involves massive hormonal changes serving many purposes (maintaining the pregnancy, remodeling the mother's physiology), and nausea could simply be a side effect of those hormones acting on the brain's nausea circuitry, with no protective function needed to explain it; the "protective" pattern might be partly read into the data after the fact, and not all women experience sickness, nor does its absence clearly predict worse outcomes, which a tight adaptation account might expect. Where do they diverge? The adaptation view predicts _functional precision_ that the byproduct view does not require: that sickness should track fetal vulnerability more tightly than hormonal levels alone would predict, that aversions should target genuine risk rather than just strong smells, and that, on average, the pattern should correlate with reproductive benefit. Careful studies probing exactly those divergences are what could move the verdict. The honest current position, as 7.3 said, is a _promising candidate adaptation_ with real but incomplete support, and the exercise's value is in feeling how a genuine, well-motivated hypothesis can still be appropriately uncertain, neither hyped nor dismissed.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 7: The Sweet Tooth and the Modern World
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

We explained the cookie. Our love of sweetness, fat, and salt is an evolved nutritional guidance system, exquisitely tuned to steer a hungry animal toward the scarce, valuable energy and nutrients of the ancestral world. The cravings that feel like weakness were, in their original setting, wisdom. The modern epidemic of diet-related harm comes not from a broken system but from a working one running in a world that violates its every assumption: this is _evolutionary mismatch_ , and the sweet tooth is its cleanest case, acing the four-part test (well-understood ancestral problem, specific adaptive logic, clear recent environmental change, confirmed detailed prediction). We used that gold standard as a measuring stick, watching how weaker mismatch claims (the anxiety story, the desk-job story) fail the same test and so deserve a lower grade, because "mismatch," like the EEA, can become a magic word that explains everything and therefore nothing. We placed pregnancy sickness in the genuinely uncertain middle, a _promising candidate adaptation_ with real but incomplete support, and practiced the calibrated in-between judgment that honest work demands. And throughout, even in this friendliest territory, we kept the firewall lit: that a craving is evolved tells us nothing about how we _ought_ to eat, and understanding the deep roots of appetite should deepen our compassion, never license judgment of ourselves or others.

The next chapter completes Part 2's tour of the body's ancient wisdom by returning to a puzzle we left open in Chapter 5: why is the mind built to make so many _false alarms_? Your snake-detector over-finds snakes; your disgust over-avoids; your fear fires before you can see. Chapter 8 reveals the beautiful logic underneath all of it, a single principle that explains why a well-designed mind should be systematically, intelligently wrong, and why your anxiety, your jealousy, and your superstitions may all be running the same ancient, sensible program. It is one of the most elegant ideas in the field, and it ties together everything in Part 2.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: The Smoke Detector in Your Head
blocks.src:
Your kitchen smoke detector is, by any strict measure, a terrible judge of fires. It shrieks when you make toast. It panics over a slightly overdone steak. The overwhelming majority of times it goes off, there is no fire at all, just a little smoke and a lot of false alarm. If you graded it as a fire-detector on accuracy, it would fail. And yet it is a brilliantly designed device, and you would be a fool to replace it with a "smarter" one that only sounded when it was _sure_. Why? Because the two mistakes it could make are not equal. A false alarm costs you a few seconds of annoyance and some waving of a dish towel. A missed alarm costs you your house and possibly your life. Faced with that brutal asymmetry, the rational design is exactly the one you have: hair-trigger, jumpy, willing to cry wolf a hundred times to avoid being silent the one time it matters.

Now here is the idea that ties together everything in Part 2 and reaches forward into the most charged chapters of the book. Your mind is full of smoke detectors. The snake-flinch that fired before you could see (Chapter 5), the disgust that recoils from harmless things (Chapter 6), the anxiety that floods you before any real threat appears, all of these may be running the same ancient, sensible logic as the device on your kitchen ceiling. They are not malfunctions. They are not stupidity. They are the predictable output of a system that has been shaped, across deep time, to make the _cheaper_ mistake when it cannot be certain. Once you see this principle, a hundred puzzling features of the mind click into place, and you understand at last why a well-built mind should be systematically, intelligently _wrong_.


### 8.1 The logic of asymmetric error

Whenever you must judge an uncertain situation and act, you can be wrong in two opposite directions. Suppose you hear a rustle in the grass. You can believe it is a predator when it is really the wind (a _false alarm_), or believe it is the wind when it is really a predator (a _miss_). You cannot eliminate both kinds of error at once when the signal is ambiguous; tuning yourself to avoid one kind necessarily makes the other kind more likely. A jumpy, suspicious mind makes few misses but many false alarms. A calm, skeptical mind makes few false alarms but the occasional deadly miss. The question evolution "asks," through the slow filter of who survived to reproduce, is: which kind of error is _cheaper_?

And here is the crucial insight: the two errors are almost never equally costly. In the rustle-in-the-grass case, a false alarm costs you a wasted sprint and a racing heart, recovered in minutes. A miss costs you your life and every descendant you might have had. When the costs are that lopsided, the optimal strategy is _not_ to be accurate. It is to be _biased_ , deliberately tilted toward making the cheap error so as to almost never make the expensive one. A mind that flinched at a hundred sticks to avoid being killed by the one snake left more descendants than a mind that calmly assessed each shape and was occasionally right about a stick while being fatally wrong about a snake. The bias is not a flaw in the design. The bias _is_ the design.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: The Smoke Detector in Your Head
blocks.src:
#### Definition: Error management theory
